cannot sink or rise to any other "reality" but just that of our impulses—for thinking is only a
relation of these impulses to one another:—are we not permitted to make the attempt and to

but as possessing the same degree of reality as our emotions themselves—as a more primitive
form of the world of emotions, in which everything still lies locked in a mighty unity, which
afterwards branches off and develops itself in organic processes (naturally also, refines and
debilitates)—as a kind of instinctive life in which all organic functions, including self-
regulation, assimilation, nutrition, secretion, and change of matter, are still synthetically
united with one another—as a primary form of life?—In the end, it is not only permitted to
make this attempt, it is commanded by the conscience of logical method. Not to assume several
kinds of causality, so long as the attempt to get along with a single one has not been pushed to

say. The question is ultimately whether we really recognize the will as operating, whether we
believe in the causality of the will; if we do so—and fundamentally our belief in this is just our

solution of the problem of generation and nutrition—it is one problem—could also be found

Til.	Of course, Marx was human and fallible. If "Capital" had never been written, there would still
have been a Socialist movement, and if it could be destroyed by criticism, the Socialist
movement would remain. Socialism is the product of economic conditions, not of a theory or a
book. "Capital" is the intellectual explanation of the genesis of Socialism, and neither its cause
nor an argument for it by which it must be judged. Hence the futility of such missions as that
undertaken by Mr. W. H. Mallock, for example, based upon the assumption that attacks upon
the text of Marx will serve to destroy or seriously hinder the living movement. Like a prophet's
rebuke to these critics, as well as to those within the ranks of the Socialist movement who
would make of the words of Marx and Engels fetters to bind the movement to a dogma, come
the words of Engels, published recently, letters in which he writes vigorously to his friend
Sorge concerning the working-class movement in England and America. Of his compatriots,
the handful of German Socialist exiles in America, who sought to make the American workers
swallow a mass of ill-digested Marxian theory, he writes, "The Germans have never
understood how to apply themselves from their theory to the lever which could set the
American masses in motion; to a great extent they do not understand the theory itself and
treat it in a doctrinaire and dogmatic fashion.... It is a credo to them, not a guide to action."
And again, "Our theory is not a dogma, but the exposition of a process of evolution, and that
process involves several successive phases." Of the English movement he writes, "And here an
instinctive Socialism is more and more taking possession of the masses which, fortunately, is
opposed to all distinct formulation according to the dogmas of one or the other so-called
organizations," and again, he condemns "the bringing down of the Marxian theory of
development to a rigid orthodoxy." The critics who hope to destroy the Socialist movement of
to-day by stringing together mistaken predictions of Marx and Engels, or who think that
Socialism is losing its grip because it is adjusting its expressions to the changed conditions

which the progress of fifty years has brought about, utterly mistake the character of the
movement. In its abandonment of the errors of Marx it is most truly Marxian—because it is
expressing life instead of repeating dogma.
Source: Socialism: A Summary and Interpretation of Socialist Principles
The passage contains direct references to Engels’ letters to Sorge and discussions about
doctrinaire Marxism.

have been a Socialist movement, and if it could be destroyed by criticism, the Socialist
movement would remain. Socialism is the product of economic conditions, not of a theory or a
book. "Capital" is the intellectual explanation of the genesis of Socialism, and neither its cause
nor an argument for it by which it must be judged. Hence the futility of such missions as that
undertaken by Mr. W. H. Mallock, for example, based upon the assumption that attacks upon
the text of Marx will serve to destroy or seriously hinder the living movement. Like a prophet's
rebuke to these critics, as well as to those within the ranks of the Socialist movement who
would make of the words of Marx and Engels fetters to bind the movement to a dogma, come
the words of Engels, published recently, letters in which he writes vigorously to his friend
Sorge concerning the working-class movement in England and America. Of his compatriots,
the handful of German Socialist exiles in America, who sought to make the American workers
swallow a mass of ill-digested Marxian theory, he writes, "The Germans have never

V.	The Union Cabinet recently cleared a legislative proposal aimed at revising an existing law
governing the sanctioned strength of the country's apex judicial institution. The proposed
amendment seeks to expand the court’s adjudicatory capacity by increasing the number of
judges, with the objective of addressing growing judicial demands and improving the efficiency
of case disposal.
It has been widely welcomed by members of the legal fraternity, who described it as a timely
step to deal with rising pendency and growing litigation before the apex court.
Many legal experts believe that increasing the capacity of higher courts can help them
function more effectively. A larger number of judges may allow courts to hear more cases,
devote greater attention to important constitutional matters, and reduce the burden on
individual judges. This, in turn, could contribute to quicker disposal of cases and a more
responsive justice system.
However, former Union Law Secretary PK Malhotra said that simply increasing the number of
judges may not bring major judicial reforms. He suggested that the government should
consider setting up regional Courts of Appeal so that the Supreme Court can focus mainly on
constitutional matters.
Overall, while legal experts have largely welcomed the Centre's decision, many believe that
increasing the number of judges must be accompanied by wider judicial reforms to effectively
tackle delays and pendency in the justice delivery system.
Source: Adapted from "President Murmu Approves Increasing Supreme Court Judge Strength,"
The Hindu.

largely reserved for national space agencies. The high costs, technological complexity, and
risks associated with space missions made it difficult for private companies to participate
meaningfully in the sector. However, this situation has begun to change as advances in
technology, greater access to investment, and supportive policy reforms have opened new
opportunities for private enterprises.
India's space sector has experienced a particularly significant transformation in recent years.
A growing number of start-ups are developing launch vehicles, satellite technologies, and
other space-based solutions. Their emergence reflects increasing confidence in the commercial
potential of the country's space ecosystem and demonstrates how innovation-driven businesses
can contribute to fields traditionally dominated by the government.

space technology company, which became one of the few Indian private space firms to attain
unicorn status after crossing a valuation of more than one billion dollars. Founded by former
scientists and engineers from the Indian space sector, the company has focused on developing
launch vehicles for small satellites. Its rise has been viewed as an important indicator of
investor confidence in India's expanding private space industry.
The achievement extends beyond financial valuation. It signals growing global interest in
India's capabilities in advanced technology and aerospace innovation. Supporters argue that
such developments can attract further investment, generate high-skilled employment, and
encourage collaboration between government agencies, research institutions, and private
companies.

As the global space economy continues to expand, the success of companies like Skyroot
Aerospace highlights the increasing role that private enterprise can play in shaping the future
of space exploration and commercial space activities.

VII. The global governing body of the Olympic Movement has approved a revised participation
framework for female sporting categories. Under the new policy, eligibility for women's events
at major international competitions will be determined through a uniform verification
mechanism. "Eligibility for any female category event at the Olympic Games or any other IOC
event, including individual and team sports, is now limited to biological females," the
International Olympic Committee said, to be determined by a mandatory gene test once in an
athlete's career.
It is unclear how many, if any, transgender women are competing at an Olympic level. No
woman who transitioned from being born male competed at the 2024 Paris Summer Games,
though weightlifter Laurel Hubbard did at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 without winning a
medal. The eligibility policy that will apply from the LA Olympics in July 2028 "protects
fairness, safety and integrity in the female category," the IOC said.
After an executive board meeting, the International Olympic Committee published a 10-page
policy document which also restricts female athletes such as two-time Olympic champion
runner Caster Semenya with medical conditions known as differences in sex development, or
DSD.

from around the world." The expert group agreed the current gene test is "the most accurate
and least intrusive method currently available." The saliva, cheek swab or blood sample
screens for "the SRY gene, a segment of DNA typically found on the Y chromosome that
initiates male sex development in utero and indicates the presence of testes/testicles."

VIII. From the very beginning, women were active participants in the events which brought about
many important changes in French society. They hoped that their involvement would
pressurise the revolutionary government to introduce measures to improve their lives. Most
women of the Third Estate had to work for a living. They worked as seamstresses or
laundresses, sold flowers, fruits and vegetables in the market, or were employed as domestic
servants in the houses of prosperous people.
Most women did not have access to education or job training. Only daughters of nobles or
wealthier members of the Third Estate could study at a convent, after which their families
arranged a marriage for them. Working women also had to care for their families. They cooked
food, fetched water, queued up for bread, and looked after children. Despite carrying out these
responsibilities, their wages were lower than those of men.
In order to discuss and voice their interests, women started their own political clubs and
newspapers. About sixty women's clubs came up in different French cities. The Society of
Revolutionary and Republican Women was the most famous among them. One of their main
demands was that women should enjoy the same political rights as men. Women were
disappointed that the Constitution of 1791 reduced them to passive citizens. They demanded
the right to vote, to be elected to the Assembly, and to hold political office. They believed that
only then would their interests be represented in the new government.
In the early years, the revolutionary government introduced several laws that helped improve
the lives of women. Along with the creation of state schools, schooling was made compulsory
for all girls. Fathers could no longer force their daughters into marriage against their will.
Marriage became a contract entered into freely and registered under civil law. Divorce was
made legal and could be applied for by both women and men. Women could now train for jobs,
become artists, or run small businesses.
Source: Adapted from India and the Contemporary World-I (History), Class IX, Chapter 1: The
French Revolution, NCERT

IX.	In the first major legislative loss for the Modi government since it came to power in 2014, the
Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeking to advance reservation of 33% seats for
women in an expanded Lok Sabha and state Assemblies and facilitate delimitation of
constituencies, was defeated in Lok Sabha Friday evening.
Of the 528 members present in the House, 298 voted in favour of the Bill and 230 opposed it,
the result well short of the two-thirds majority needed for a Constitutional amendment Bill to
clear the House.
The amended women's quota Bill was put to vote after a marathon two-day debate during
which Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah urged members to
support the proposed legislation, and cautioned the Opposition that women of the country
were watching their intent and would not forgive them if they were denied reservation.
The Opposition, in turn, accused the government of using the women's reservation issue to
push for a delimitation exercise to help the BJP by redrawing the country's electoral map and
adversely impacting the representation of southern states in Lok Sabha. The rejected bill
sought to fast-track the implementation of women's reservation and permit delimitation

without waiting for a fresh Census. It aimed to amend provisions linked to the Nari Shakti
Vandan Adhiniyam, which provides 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and
state legislatures.
Source: Adapted from "Women's Quota Bill Defeated in Lok Sabha; Fails to Get Two-Thirds
Majority,” The New Indian Express (Apr. 17, 2026)

questions.stimulus:
XII. The Supreme Court’s judgment in J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency v. Rash Builders
India Private Limited revisited the distinction between the “seat” and “venue” of arbitration
and clarified how this distinction determines the supervisory jurisdiction of courts under the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The dispute arose from infrastructure contracts
executed in Jammu and Kashmir between the Jammu and Kashmir Economic Reconstruction
Agency (JKERA) and Rash Builders India Pvt. Ltd. After disagreements concerning
contractual claims, arbitration proceedings were initiated.
Initially, the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir appointed a sole arbitrator. Subsequently, by
an order dated 26 March 2016, the arbitral tribunal recorded that, with the consent of both
parties, Srinagar would be the “seat” of arbitration while New Delhi would merely function as
the “venue” for conducting hearings. The proceedings were later conducted in New Delhi for
convenience, and the arbitral award was also pronounced there.
After the award was delivered, JKERA filed a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act before the Jammu and Kashmir High Court seeking to challenge the award.
However, the High Court returned the petition on the ground that since hearings were

conducted and the award was rendered in New Delhi, courts in Delhi alone possessed
jurisdiction. JKERA challenged this conclusion before the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court observed that arbitration law consistently recognizes a distinction
between “seat” and “venue.” According to the Court, the seat of arbitration constitutes the
juridical home of the arbitration and determines which court exercises supervisory jurisdiction
over arbitral proceedings. The venue, by contrast, is merely a geographically convenient place
where hearings may be conducted. Therefore, the mere fact that hearings occur or an award is
delivered at a particular location does not automatically transfer jurisdiction to courts situated
there.
The Court emphasized that once parties expressly designate a seat of arbitration, courts at
that place alone possess exclusive jurisdiction over arbitration-related proceedings, including
challenges to arbitral awards. Such designation operates similarly to an exclusive jurisdiction
clause in commercial contracts. The Court further held that the seat remains fixed and
immutable unless the parties expressly agree to alter it later. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Applying these principles, the Supreme Court held that Srinagar remained the juridical seat
because the parties had expressly agreed to it. The Court rejected the respondent’s argument
that the award mentioning New Delhi as the “place of arbitration” changed the seat. According
to the Court, stray recitals in an arbitral award cannot override the express agreement of
parties. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and restored
JKERA’s Section 34 proceedings before the Jammu and Kashmir High Court. The judgment
reaffirmed party autonomy, certainty in arbitral procedure, and the central importance of the
juridical seat in determining court jurisdiction.

XIII. The doctrine of constructive res judicata is an important extension of the principle of res
judicata embodied under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC). While the
traditional rule of res judicata bars the re-litigation of issues that have already been directly
and substantially decided between the same parties, constructive res judicata prevents parties
from raising matters in subsequent proceedings that they “might and ought” to have raised in
earlier litigation. The doctrine is primarily incorporated through Explanation IV to Section 11
CPC and is closely connected with Order II Rule 2 of the CPC.
The rationale behind the doctrine is based upon public policy, judicial economy, and the need
to ensure finality in litigation. Courts seek to prevent parties from splitting claims or
withholding grounds strategically in order to initiate multiple rounds of litigation over the
same dispute. The principle is therefore intended to protect opposing parties from repeated
harassment and to prevent wastage of judicial time. The Supreme Court has repeatedly
emphasized that litigation must eventually attain finality, since endless challenges undermine
public confidence in the judicial process.
Recently, the Supreme Court examined the doctrine while considering a dispute concerning
property rights where a respondent attempted to claim reliefs in a later suit that could and
should have been sought in an earlier proceeding itself. The Court observed that the dispute
regarding the parties’ rights already existed at the time of the first suit, and therefore all
connected reliefs ought to have been claimed together. Since the respondent was fully aware of
the rival claim during the earlier proceedings, the subsequent suit was barred by constructive
res judicata and by the principles underlying Order II Rule 2 CPC. The Court held that parties
cannot be permitted to re-agitate issues by merely altering the form of relief sought in later
litigation.

Karnataka (2011), the Supreme Court clarified that constructive res judicata may apply even
to writ petitions. The Court reasoned that litigants cannot repeatedly invoke constitutional
remedies on grounds that could reasonably have been urged earlier. However, courts have also

recognized that the doctrine should not be applied mechanically in exceptional situations
involving changed circumstances, continuing violations, or issues affecting personal liberty.
Thus, constructive res judicata represents a balance between two competing concerns:
ensuring fairness to litigants while also preserving certainty, consistency, and finality in
judicial proceedings. The doctrine discourages fragmented litigation and promotes efficient
administration of justice by compelling parties to present their entire case at the earliest
available opportunity.

XV. In a significant ruling on personal liberty and individual autonomy, the Kerala High Court
has held that parents cannot invoke the writ of habeas corpus merely because they disapprove
of their adult daughters’ decision to join a religious congregation and lead a life of celibacy.
The case, Joju George and Ors. v. State of Kerala and Ors. (2026), was decided by a Division
Bench comprising Justice A.K. Jayasankaran Nambiar and Justice Jobin Sebastian of the
Kerala High Court.
The petition was filed by three parents alleging that their daughters, aged 21, 26 and 30, were
being illegally detained by members of a religious congregation known as the Monastery of
Holy Ruah (MHR). According to the petitioners, their daughters had joined the congregation
when it was recognised by the Archdiocese of Thrissur. However, after the Archdiocese
dissolved the congregation in 2023, the parents claimed that their daughters continued to
remain there under coercion.
The petitioners argued that parental guidance and authority over children should not be
brushed aside merely because the children had attained majority, contending that courts
should intervene where decisions taken by adult children were immature or influenced. The
Court rejected this reasoning. It noted that police enquiries revealed that the daughters
themselves signed statements affirming that they were voluntarily continuing with the
congregation. Accordingly, the Court held that parental disagreement could not justify judicial
intervention through habeas corpus.
A central theme of the judgment was individual autonomy. The Bench observed that the
choice of the alleged detenus with regard to their beliefs or the congregation that they must
join is a matter that rests exclusively within the private domain of the individual concerned,
warning that interference by the State in such matters would have a chilling effect on the
exercise of constitutional freedoms by the individual concerned. The Court cautioned that, as
"sentinels on the qui vive", this Court must tread with caution when called upon to issue writs
in the nature of Habeas Corpus alleging illegal detention.
In its concluding observation, the Bench held that the mere disgruntlement of a parent with
the decision of his adult daughter, who has chosen a life of celibacy by responding to the call of
the Divine, cannot be the basis for the issuance of a writ of Habeas Corpus. The ruling
reinforces a broader judicial trend in India protecting the autonomy of adults to make personal
choices regarding faith and lifestyle, free from parental or State coercion.

questions.stimulus:
XIX. Can a society genuinely claim to oppose dowry while continuing to treat marriage as the
highest marker of respectability? What would it mean to respond to dowry deaths not with
fleeting outrage, but with the courage to imagine different ways of living and belonging? It is
almost always the most extreme forms of violence that disturb the public conscience. Images
spread, testimonies emerge, anger builds, and demands for justice grow louder. Grief appears
collective briefly. Yet the moment passes, almost as predictably. Outrage fades while the social
world that produces such violence remains largely unchanged and even celebrated. Marriage
continues to be presented as aspiration, security, and inevitability, even as financial
transactions surrounding it stay deeply normalised. Dowry may be publicly condemned in
principle, yet it is quietly repackaged through the language of gifts, family honour, or the
assumption that a man, as primary earner, deserves material compensation. Weddings
function as performances of social worth, where financial display is not merely tolerated but
actively admired. Conversations about daughters still carry the language of burden and
responsibility, revealing how deeply marriage remains tied to economic and social anxieties.
Marital violence, therefore, cannot be understood as an exception alone; it grows from a
structure whose underlying logic society continuously justifies. Women enter marriage under

deeply unequal conditions, more likely to give up careers, absorb unpaid care work, and bear
the greater burden of maintaining family harmony. The expectation of sacrifice remains
attached to women, even when softened through the language of compromise or culture. This
is perhaps the central limitation of outrage: it allows society to condemn violence without
examining the conditions that make it normal. Violence is treated as the moral failure of
certain individuals, rather than as a symptom of a social order in which marriage remains tied
to economic exchange, gendered labour, and the preservation of caste hierarchies. Marriage
has historically functioned as far more than a personal relationship. It has operated
simultaneously as an economic arrangement, a mechanism for preserving social boundaries,
and a system through which families negotiate status and security. Financial transaction,
therefore, does not appear accidental to marriage; it is embedded within its very logic. The
violence is not confined to visible brutality alone. It is present in quieter pressures: the social
anxiety surrounding unmarried women, the normalisation of women's endless adjustment as
virtue, and the absence of legitimate alternatives. What society lacks is not simply better laws
or louder condemnation, but the imagination to envision ways of living in which dignity,
belonging, and security do not depend upon marriage.

questions.stimulus:
XX. In his seminal 1998 treatise, James C. Scott argued that sovereign power invariably begins by
rendering its subjects "legible" — comprehensible, cataloguable, and therefore controllable.
The East India Company operationalised precisely this logic three centuries ago, conquering
the subcontinent not through military supremacy alone, but through the meticulous reduction
of India's civilisational complexity into predictable administrative data points, after which
colonial subjugation became a bureaucratic inevitability. Today, an analogous but far more
insidious architecture of domination is crystallising — one encoded not in imperial ledgers but
in algorithmic infrastructure. India's Digital Public Infrastructure, celebrated internationally
as a sovereign achievement in technological transparency, has paradoxically engineered the
conditions for a new form of extractive colonialism. In the contemporary global order, a
nation's legibility is no longer a precondition for prosperity; it is a blueprint for dispossession.
Offshore AI clusters operated by foreign hedge funds and transnational capital conglomerates
are systematically ingesting Indian transactional data — every UPI payment, every logistical
fluctuation, every consumer search pattern — to construct predictive models of extraordinary
granularity. The April 2026 Global Data Flow Report estimates annual value leakage
attributable to this predictive arbitrage at approximately $150 billion, constituting what must
be recognised as algorithmic colonialism. When an adversary's computational architecture can
anticipate your economic behaviour with greater precision than your own policymakers,
sovereign negotiating capacity is rendered structurally illusory. Against this epistemic
dispossession, the author proposes a radical defensive doctrine: Neural Satyagraha — a
deliberate, institutionalised refusal to remain algorithmically legible. Analogous to Gandhi's
principled non-cooperation with exploitative legal structures, Neural Satyagraha demands the
intentional cultivation of strategic opacity through what the author provocatively reframes as

organised entropy. India's improvisational tradition — historically derided as inefficiency —
becomes, within this framework, its most formidable geopolitical asset, since jugaad-style
unpredictability constitutes precisely the variable that linear, Western-trained predictive
models cannot adequately simulate. Practically, this doctrine requires sovereign noise
injection into global data streams, privacy-preserving obfuscation protocols, and reciprocal
opacity clauses embedded within future trade negotiations. India's trajectory toward a thirty-
trillion-dollar economy by 2047 ultimately depends not upon maximising algorithmic
transparency, but upon cultivating the one resource that computation cannot commodify —
irreducible human intuition.

questions.stimulus:
XXVI. In 2025, five National Law Universities—NLSIU Bangalore, NLU Delhi, NALSAR Hyderabad,
NLU Jodhpur and NLU Bhopal—formed the National Law Research Consortium (NALRC) to
develop artificial intelligence tools for legal research, judicial analytics and policy drafting.
The project continued for three years. Since universities joined the consortium at different
points of time, the final commercialization revenue generated by the project was distributed
according to each university's effective contribution ratio, defined as: Number of Researchers x
Duration of Participation. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The consortium report stated that NLSIU Bangalore deployed 334% more researchers than
NLU Delhi. NALSAR Hyderabad deployed 25% more researchers than NLSIU Bangalore.
NLU Jodhpur deployed 20% fewer researchers than NALSAR Hyderabad. The number of
researchers deployed by NLU Jodhpur and NLU Bhopal was in the ratio 1/4: 1/5. The total
number of researchers from all the law universities combined is 96. NLSIU Bangalore and
NLU Delhi participated throughout the three-year duration of the project. NALSAR
Hyderabad joined after the completion of the first year. NLU Jodhpur joined six months after
NALSAR Hyderabad entered the consortium. NLU Bhopal joined after the completion of the
second year. At the conclusion of the project, the consortium generated %4.02 crore through
licensing agreements and commercialization of research outputs. The revenue was distributed
among participating universities according to their effective contribution ratio.
